visuals.title: Where DKA shows itself
visuals.text: Pancreas fails to make insulin; kidneys lose water and electrolytes; lungs blow off CO2; brain gets confused.

visual.title: Venous pH
visual.caption: All grades need blood ketones >3 mmol/L and urine ketones >2+.
visual.label: pH 7.15 = moderate

visuals.title: Order of treatment
nodes: SC insulin once resolved and eating

visual.title: During treatment
visual.caption: Glucose falls first; insulin continues with 10% glucose until ketones are <0.6.

visuals.title: Why patients are dry
nodes: No insulin: glucose cannot enter cells
Total body K low, serum K normal/high

glossary.Type 1: Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, so the body makes little or no insulin.
glossary.Hyperglycaemia: Blood glucose that is higher than normal.
glossary.Hypoglycaemia: Blood glucose that is too low, causing sweating, confusion and, if severe, seizures or coma.
glossary.Insulin deficiency: Too little insulin, so cells cannot take up glucose and fat breakdown is no longer switched off.
glossary.Acetone: A ketone body breathed out in DKA, giving the breath a fruity or pear-drop smell.
glossary.Dehydration: Loss of body water greater than intake, causing thirst, dry mucosa, tachycardia and low blood pressure.
glossary.Haemodynamically unstable: Circulation is failing: low blood pressure, fast heart rate or poor organ perfusion.
glossary.Electrolytes: Charged salts in the blood, such as sodium, potassium and chloride, that control fluid balance and nerve and muscle function.
glossary.Ketone bodies: Acidic fuels (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) the liver makes from fatty acids when insulin is lacking.
glossary.Free fatty acids: Fatty acids released from stored fat by lipolysis; the liver turns them into ketones.
glossary.Respiratory compensation: Changing breathing to correct a pH problem; in metabolic acidosis, breathing deeper to blow off CO2.
glossary.Osmotic shifts: Movement of water across cell membranes when the concentration of dissolved particles changes on one side.
glossary.Endocrinologist: A specialist doctor in hormone conditions such as diabetes.
glossary.SC: Subcutaneous: given by injection into the fat just under the skin.
glossary.Subcutaneous: Into the fat layer just under the skin, the usual route for regular insulin injections.
glossary.IV: Intravenous: given directly into a vein.
glossary.Dextrose: Another name for glucose, given in IV fluids to prevent hypoglycaemia.
glossary.Infusion: A drug or fluid given continuously into a vein over a set time.
glossary.Fixed-rate: A set insulin dose per hour based on body weight, not adjusted to each glucose reading.
glossary.Long-acting insulin: Background (basal) insulin that works for about 24 hours; continued during DKA treatment.
glossary.Short-acting insulin: Mealtime insulin that acts quickly for a few hours; stopped while the IV insulin runs.
glossary.Seizures: Fits caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
glossary.Altered mental status: Any change in alertness, behaviour or thinking, from confusion to coma.
glossary.Serum: The liquid part of blood after clotting; serum levels are what blood tests measure.
glossary.Total body potassium: All the potassium in the body, mostly inside cells, which can be low even when blood potassium looks normal.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity from electrodes on the skin.
glossary.T waves: The part of the ECG showing ventricular repolarisation; shape changes with potassium level.
glossary.Electrolyte loss: Salts such as sodium and potassium lost in the urine along with water.
glossary.Urine ketones: Ketones detected on a urine dipstick, graded from + to ++++.
glossary.Ketosis: Raised ketones in the body without acidosis.
glossary.Acidosis: Too much acid in the blood, so the pH falls below normal (below 7.35).
glossary.Nausea: The feeling of needing to vomit.
glossary.Resolution: Recovery from DKA, defined as pH >7.3, ketones <0.6 mmol/L and bicarbonate >15 mmol/L.
glossary.Capillary blood gas: Blood gas test on a small sample from a finger or heel prick.
glossary.Capillary blood ketones: Ketone level measured from a finger-prick blood sample with a bedside meter.
glossary.Gold standard: The best available test for confirming a diagnosis.
glossary.Monitoring: Repeated checking of observations and blood results, hourly in DKA, to guide treatment.
glossary.NaCl: Sodium chloride: salt; 0.9% NaCl is normal saline, the first fluid used in DKA.
glossary.KCl: Potassium chloride, added to IV fluids to replace potassium.
glossary.mmol/L: Millimoles per litre: the unit for concentrations of glucose, ketones and electrolytes in blood.
glossary.Saline: Salt solution given IV; normal saline is 0.9% sodium chloride.
glossary.Underlying precipitant: The trigger that started the DKA, such as infection or missed insulin, which must also be treated.
glossary.Neurology: Function of the brain and nerves, such as consciousness, speech and movement.
glossary.CO2: Carbon dioxide; breathing it off removes acid and raises blood pH.
